title: Your Body Speaks Before You Do
excerpt: Getting into better shape has changed more than my appearance. I've noticed a difference in how I carry myself, how I feel walking into a room and, perhaps, how other people respond to me. But the biggest change isn't what my body says to other people - it's what getting fit has taught me about myself.
content:
Here's an uncomfortable thought: people have already formed some kind of impression of you before you've said a word.

They see your clothes, your posture, your energy and, whether we like it or not, your body.

Since getting myself into some sort of shape, I've noticed that people seem to respond to me differently. It's subtle. Nobody announces, "You look like you work out." It's more in the small things. I sometimes feel more confident in conversations and more comfortable walking into a room, and there seems to be a slightly different level of attention in some interactions.

Maybe some of that is in my head. In fact, I'm sure some of it is. But I think some of it comes from something simpler: I carry myself differently now. And that's made me think about what our bodies communicate before we open our mouths.

## Your body tells part of your story

Nobody sees the mornings when you get out of bed instead of hitting snooze. They don't see the workouts you nearly skipped, the meals you prepared, the walks you went on when you couldn't really be bothered, or the decisions you made to look after yourself when nobody was watching. They just see the result: a visible consequence of hundreds of decisions nobody else saw.

That's something I've started to appreciate about fitness. Losing fat or building muscle is nice, but it's the end result of something else. Getting into better shape means repeatedly doing things that are good for you, even when you don't feel like it, and eventually you realise you're capable of keeping promises to yourself.

## It's not about impressing people

There's a danger in treating any of this as a way to win other people's approval, and that isn't what I mean.

You shouldn't train because you think you're not good enough as you are, or spend your life worrying about whether strangers think you look good. You should look after yourself because you're worth looking after.

Every time you keep a small promise to yourself, whether that's getting to the gym, going for a walk, eating reasonably well or going to bed instead of staying up late for no reason, you build a little more trust in yourself. When you keep proving that you'll do what you said you would, you start to see yourself as someone who can be relied on. That's worth a lot more than bigger arms or a smaller waist.

## Start with the easy stuff

You don't need to transform yourself tomorrow. Some of the things that make the biggest difference are surprisingly basic:

- Wear clothes that fit properly. They don't need to be expensive. Being clean, well presented and wearing something that fits you can make more difference than a wardrobe full of designer clothes.
- Stand up straight. If you've spent years hunched over a laptop or looking down at your phone, just becoming more conscious of how you carry yourself can change how you feel.
- Move every day. Go to the gym, walk, run, cycle or play a sport. It doesn't have to be complicated.
- Get your sleep under control.

None of that is revolutionary, and I think that's why it works. Personal development often gets presented as if you need an elaborate system to reinvent yourself, when a lot of the time it's about doing the basics consistently.

Most of all, keep the small promises you make to yourself. If you say you're going to train, train. If you say you'll get up at a certain time, get up. If you decide to look after yourself a bit better, follow through. You don't have to be perfect. You just need to become someone you can rely on.

## The bigger change

Yes, people judge appearances. That's part of being human. But I don't think the answer is to spend your life worrying about what everyone else thinks. The more interesting goal is to become someone *you* respect.

Looking back, one of the unexpected benefits of getting into shape has been how I feel walking into a room: how I carry myself, and how comfortable I am in my own skin. Maybe some of that is how other people see me, but I'm pretty sure a lot of it is how I now see myself.

If your body says anything before you speak, I'd like it to be something like: "I look after myself, I make commitments to myself, and I follow through." Keep doing the basics and keeping those promises, and over time the person people see on the outside starts to reflect the one you've been building on the inside.
